section.heading: 4.1. Maximum and Minimum Values
section.paragraph: Some of the most important applications of differential calculus are optimization problems, in which we are required to find the optimal (best) way of doing something. Here are examples of such problems that we will solve in this chapter:

list.item: What is the shape of a can that minimizes manufacturing costs?
What is the maximum acceleration of a spacecraft? (This is an important question for the astronauts who have to withstand the effects of acceleration.)
What is the radius of a contracted windpipe that expels air most rapidly during a cough?
At what angle should blood vessels branch so as to minimize the energy expended by the heart in pumping blood?

section.paragraph: These problems can be reduced to finding the maximum or minimum values of a function. Let’s first explain exactly what we mean by maximum and minimum values.
section.heading: Absolute and Local Extreme Values
section.paragraph: We see that the highest point on the graph of the function $$f$$ shown in Figure 1 is the point $$\left( {3,5} \right)$$ . In other words, the largest value of $$f$$ is $$f(3) = 5$$ . Likewise, the smallest value is $$f(6) = 2$$ . We say that $$f(3) = 5$$ is the absolute maximum of $$f$$ and $$f(6) = 2$$ is the absolute minimum. In general, we use the following definition.

The y axis is displayed from negative 1 to 6 in increments of 1 unit. The curve begins at the point (1, 3), goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point at (3, 5), goes down and to the right becoming concave up, reaches its low point at (6, 2), again goes up and ends at the point (7, 3).

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Let $$c$$ be a number in the domain $$D$$ of a function $$f$$ . Then $$f(c)$$ is the

list.item: absolute maximum value of $$f$$ on $$D$$ if $$f(c) \geqslant f(x)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$D$$ .
absolute minimum value of $$f$$ on $$D$$ if $$f(c) \leqslant f(x)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$D$$ .

section.paragraph: An absolute maximum or minimum is sometimes called a global maximum or minimum. The maximum and minimum values of $$f$$ are called extreme values of $$f$$ .

Figure 2 shows the graph of a function $$f$$ with absolute maximum at $$d$$ and absolute minimum at $$a$$ . Note that $$\left( {d,f(d)} \right)$$ is the highest point on the graph and $$\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ is the lowest point. In Figure 2, if we consider only values of $$x$$ near $$b$$ [for instance, if we restrict our attention to the interval $$\left( {a,c} \right)$$ ], then $$f(b)$$ is the largest of those values of $$f(x)$$ and is called a local maximum value of $$f$$ . Likewise, $$f(c)$$ is called a local minimum value of $$f$$ because $$f(c) \leqslant f(x)$$ for $$x$$ near $$c$$ [in the interval $$\left( {b,d} \right)$$ , for instance]. The function $$f$$ also has a local minimum at $$e$$ . In general, we have the following definition.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The number $$f(c)$$ is a

list.item: local maximum value of $$f$$ if $$f(c) \geqslant f(x)$$ when $$x$$ is near $$c$$ .
local minimum value of $$f$$ if $$f(c) \leqslant f(x)$$ when $$x$$ is near $$c$$ .

section.paragraph: In Definition 2 (and elsewhere), if we say that something is true near $$c$$ , we mean that it is true on some open interval containing $$c$$ . (Thus a local maximum or minimum can’t occur at an endpoint.) For instance, in Figure 3 we see that $$f(4) = 5$$ is a local minimum because it’s the smallest value of $$f$$ on the interval $$I$$ . It’s not the absolute minimum because $$f(x)$$ takes on smaller values when $$x$$ is near $$12$$ (in the interval $$K$$ , for instance). In fact $$f(12) = 3$$ is both a local minimum and the absolute minimum. Similarly, $$f(8) = 7$$ is a local maximum, but not the absolute maximum because $$f$$ takes on larger values near $$1$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: If $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ , then $$f(x) \geqslant f(0)$$ because $$x^{2} \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ . Therefore $$f(0) = 0$$ is the absolute (and local) minimum value of $$f$$ . This corresponds to the fact that the origin is the lowest point on the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ . (See Figure 6.) However, there is no highest point on the parabola and so this function has no maximum value.

section.paragraph: We have seen that some functions have extreme values, whereas others do not. The following theorem gives conditions under which a function is guaranteed to possess extreme values.

note.title: The Extreme Value Theorem
note.heading: The Extreme Value Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is continuous on a closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$f$$ attains an absolute maximum value $$f(c)$$ and an absolute minimum value $$f(d)$$ at some numbers $$c$$ and $$d$$ in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .

section.paragraph: The Extreme Value Theorem is illustrated in Figure 8. Note that an extreme value can be taken on more than once. Although the Extreme Value Theorem is intuitively very plausible, it is difficult to prove and so we omit the proof.

section.paragraph: The function $$f$$ whose graph is shown in Figure 9 is defined on the closed interval $$\lbrack 0,2\rbrack$$ but has no maximum value. (Notice that the range of $$f$$ is $$\lbrack 0,3)$$ . The function takes on values arbitrarily close to $$3$$ , but never actually attains the value $$3$$ .) This does not contradict the Extreme Value Theorem because $$f$$ is not continuous. [Nonetheless, a discontinuous function could have maximum and minimum values. See Exercise 13(b).]

The function $$g$$ shown in Figure 10 is continuous on the open interval $$(0,2)$$ but has neither a maximum nor a minimum value. [The range of $$g$$ is $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ . The function takes on arbitrarily large values.] This does not contradict the Extreme Value Theorem because the interval $$(0,2)$$ is not closed.
section.heading: Critical Numbers and the Closed Interval Method
section.paragraph: The Extreme Value Theorem says that a continuous function on a closed interval has a maximum value and a minimum value, but it does not tell us how to find these extreme values. Notice in Figure 8 that the absolute maximum and minimum values that are between $$a$$ and $$b$$ occur at local maximum or minimum values, so we start by looking for local extreme values.

Figure 11 shows the graph of a function $$f$$ with a local maximum at $$c$$ and a local minimum at $$d$$ . It appears that at the maximum and minimum points the tangent lines are horizontal and therefore each has slope $$0$$ . We know that the derivative is the slope of the tangent line, so it appears that $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(d) = 0$$ . The following theorem says that this is always true for differentiable functions.

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The positive x axis is displayed with tick marks c and d in the order from left to right. The curve goes up and to the right from the second quadrant, crosses the y axis, becomes concave down, and reaches its high point at x = c. This high point is labeled (c, f(c)). It then goes down and to the right, becoming concave up, reaches its low point labeled (d, f(d)), and then goes up and to the right. A horizontal tangent is drawn above the high point and touches it exactly once at (c, f(c)). Another horizontal tangent is drawn below the curve and touches it exactly once at (d, f(d)). Vertical segments from tick marks c and d reach the curve.

note.title: Fermat’s Theorem
note.heading: Fermat’s Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ has a local maximum or minimum at $$c$$ , and if $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ exists, then $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ .

note.title: Proof
note.heading: Proof
note.paragraph: Suppose, for the sake of definiteness, that $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ . Then, according to Definition 2, $$f(c) \geqslant f(x)$$ if $$x$$ is sufficiently close to $$c$$ . This implies that if $$h$$ is sufficiently close to $$0$$ , with $$h$$ being positive or negative, then
$$f(c) \geqslant f\left( {c + h} \right)$$
and therefore
$$f\left( {c + h} \right) - f(c) \leqslant 0$$
We can divide both sides of an inequality by a positive number. Thus, if $$h > 0$$ and $$h$$ is sufficiently small, we have
$$\frac{f\left( {c + h} \right) - f(c)}{h} \leqslant 0$$
Taking the right-hand limit of both sides of this inequality (using Theorem 2.3.2), we get
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{f\left( {c + h} \right) - f(c)}{h} \leqslant {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{+}}}_{}0 = 0$$
But since $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ exists, we have
$$f^{\prime}(c) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {c + h} \right) - f(c)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{f\left( {c + h} \right) - f(c)}{h}$$
and so we have shown that $$f^{\prime}(c) \leqslant 0$$ .
If $$h < 0$$ , then the direction of the inequality (5) is reversed when we divide by $$h$$ :
$$\frac{f\left( {c + h} \right) - f(c)}{h} \geqslant 0$$
So, taking the left-hand limit, we have
$$f^{\prime}(c) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {c + h} \right) - f(c)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{-}}\frac{f\left( {c + h} \right) - f(c)}{h} \geqslant 0$$
We have shown that $$f^{\prime}(c) \geqslant 0$$ and also that $$f^{\prime}(c) \leqslant 0$$ . Since both of these inequalities must be true, the only possibility is that $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ .
We have proved Fermat’s Theorem for the case of a local maximum. The case of a local minimum can be proved in a similar manner, or see Exercise 81 for an alternate method.

section.paragraph: The following examples caution us against reading too much into Fermat’s Theorem: we can’t expect to locate extreme values simply by setting $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ and solving for $$x$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: If $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ , then $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2}$$ , so $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ . But $$f$$ has no maximum or minimum at $$0$$ , as you can see from its graph in Figure 12. (Or observe that $$x^{3} > 0$$ for $$x > 0$$ but $$x^{3} < 0$$ for $$x < 0$$ .) The fact that $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ simply means that the curve $$y = x^{3}$$ has a horizontal tangent at $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ . Instead of having a maximum or minimum at $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , the curve crosses its horizontal tangent there.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: The function $$f(x) = |x|$$ has its (local and absolute) minimum value at $$0$$ , but that value can’t be found by setting $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ because, as was shown in Example 2.8.5, $$f^{\prime}(0)$$ does not exist. (See Figure 13.)

The function y = abs(x) enters the second quadrant at the top left of the viewing window, goes linearly down and to the right, reaches the origin, then goes linearly up and to the right in the first quadrant, mirroring its earlier path.

section.paragraph: Warning Examples 5 and 6 show that we must be careful when using Fermat’s Theorem. Example 5 demonstrates that even when $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ there need not be a maximum or minimum at $$c$$ . (In other words, the converse of Fermat’s Theorem is false in general.) Furthermore, there may be an extreme value even when $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ does not exist (as in Example 6).

Fermat’s Theorem does suggest that we should at least start looking for extreme values of $$f$$ at the numbers $$c$$ where $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ or where $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ does not exist. Such numbers are given a special name.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A critical number of a function $$f$$ is a number $$c$$ in the domain of $$f$$ such that either $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ or $$f^{\prime}(c)$$ does not exist.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Find the critical numbers of

list.item: $$f(x) = x^{3 \slash 5}\left( {4 - x} \right)$$ .

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: The derivative of $$f$$ is $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2} - 6x = 3x(x - 2)$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ exists for all $$x$$ , the only critical numbers of $$f$$ occur when $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ , that is, when $$x = 0$$ or $$x = 2$$ .

First note that the domain of $$f$$ is $$\mathbb{R}$$ . The Product Rule gives $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {x^{3 \slash 5}\left( {- 1} \right) + \left( {4 - x} \right)\left( {\frac{3}{5}x^{- 2 \slash 5}} \right) = - x^{3 \slash 5} + \frac{3\left( {4 - x} \right)}{5x^{2 \slash 5}}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\frac{- 5x + 3\left( {4 - x} \right)}{5x^{2 \slash 5}} = \frac{12 - 8x}{5x^{2 \slash 5}}}} \end{array}$$ [The same result could be obtained by first writing $$f(x) = 4x^{3 \slash 5} - x^{8 \slash 5}$$ .] Therefore $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ if $$12 - 8x = 0$$ , that is, $$x = \frac{3}{2}$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ does not exist when $$x = 0$$ . Thus the critical numbers are $$\frac{3}{2}$$ and $$0$$ .

example.paragraph: Figure 14 shows a graph of the function $$f$$ in Example 7(b). It supports our answer because there is a horizontal tangent when $$x = 1.5$$ [where $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ ] and a vertical tangent when $$x = 0$$ [where $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is undefined].

The curve enters the viewing window in the third quadrant at approximately (negative 0.3, negative 2), goes up and to the right, initially concave up as it veers toward the y axis, and briefly levels out at the origin while following a linear vertical path. section.paragraph: In terms of critical numbers, Fermat’s Theorem can be rephrased as follows (compare Definition 6 with Theorem 4):
If $$f$$ has a local maximum or minimum at $$c$$ , then $$c$$ is a critical number of $$f$$ .

To find an absolute maximum or minimum of a continuous function on a closed interval, we note that either it is local [in which case it occurs at a critical number by (7)] or it occurs at an endpoint of the interval, as we see from the examples in Figure 8. Thus the following three-step procedure always works.

note.title: The Closed Interval Method
note.heading: The Closed Interval Method
note.paragraph: To find the absolute maximum and minimum values of a continuous function $$f$$ on a closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ :

list.item: Find the values of $$f$$ at the critical numbers of $$f$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
Find the values of $$f$$ at the endpoints of the interval.
The largest of the values from Steps 1 and 2 is the absolute maximum value; the smallest of these values is the absolute minimum value.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function
$${f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1} {- \frac{1}{2} \leqslant x \leqslant 4}$$
Solution Since $$f$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {- \frac{1}{2},4} \right\rbrack$$ , we can use the Closed Interval Method.

Example 7(a) we found the critical numbers $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 2$$ . Notice that each of these critical numbers lies in the interval $$\left\lbrack {- \frac{1}{2},4} \right\rbrack$$ . The values of $$f$$ at these critical numbers are
The values of $$f$$ at the endpoints of the interval are
Comparing these four numbers, we see that the absolute maximum value is $$f(4) = 17$$ and the absolute minimum value is $$f(2) = - 3$$ .
In this example the absolute maximum occurs at an endpoint, whereas the absolute minimum occurs at a critical number. The graph of $$f$$ is sketched in Figure 15.

section.paragraph: With graphing software or a graphing calculator it is possible to estimate maximum and minimum values very easily. But, as the next example shows, calculus is needed to find the exact values.

example.heading: Example 9

list.item: (a) Use a calculator or computer to estimate the absolute minimum and maximum values of the function $${f(x) = x - 2\sin x},{0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi}$$ .
(b) Use calculus to find the exact minimum and maximum values.

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) Figure 16 shows a graph of $$f$$ in the viewing rectangle $$\left\lbrack {0,2\pi} \right\rbrack$$ by $$\left\lbrack {- 1,8} \right\rbrack$$ . The absolute maximum value is about $$6.97$$ and it occurs when $$x \approx 5.24$$ . Similarly, the absolute minimum value is about $$- 0.68$$ and it occurs when $$x \approx 1.05$$ . It is possible to get more accurate numerical estimates, but for exact values we must use calculus. Figure 16 Details A curve is graphed on a graphing calculator window screen. The horizontal axis is displayed from 0 to 2 pi and the vertical axis is displayed from negative 1 to 8. The curve begins at the origin, goes down and to the right in the fourth quadrant, concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (pi/3, negative 0.6), then goes up and to the right through the approximate point (1.9, 0), becoming concave down, reaches its high point at approximately (5 pi/3, 6.97), and then goes down and to the right, exits the viewing window at approximately (2 pi, 6.4).

(b) The function $$f(x) = x - 2\sin x$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {0,2\pi} \right\rbrack$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1 - 2\cos x$$ , we have $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$\cos x = \frac{1}{2}$$ and this occurs when $$x = \pi \slash 3$$ or $$5\pi \slash 3$$ . The values of $$f$$ at these critical numbers are $$f\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right) = \frac{\pi}{3} - 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3} \approx - 0.684853$$ and $$f\left( {5\pi \slash 3} \right) = \frac{5\pi}{3} - 2\sin\frac{5\pi}{3} = \frac{5\pi}{3} + \sqrt{3} \approx 6.968039$$ The values of $$f$$ at the endpoints are $$f(0) = 0 f\left( {2\pi} \right) = 2\pi \approx 6.28$$ Comparing these four numbers and using the Closed Interval Method, we see that the absolute minimum value is $$f\left( {\pi \slash 3} \right) = \pi \slash 3 - \sqrt{3}$$ and the absolute maximum value is $$f\left( {5\pi \slash 3} \right) = 5\pi \slash 3 + \sqrt{3}$$ . The values from part (a) serve as a check on our work.

example.heading: Example 10
example.paragraph: The Hubble Space Telescope was deployed on April 24, 1990, by the space shuttle Discovery. A model for the velocity of the shuttle during this mission, from liftoff at $$t = 0$$ until the solid rocket boosters were jettisoned at $$t = 126{seconds}$$ , is given by
(in feet per second). Using this model, estimate the absolute maximum and minimum values of the acceleration of the shuttle between liftoff and the jettisoning of the boosters.

image.alt: A photo shows a space shuttle orbiting the Earth in space.

example.paragraph: Solution We are asked for the extreme values not of the given velocity function, but rather of the acceleration function. So we first need to differentiate to find the acceleration:
We now apply the Closed Interval Method to the continuous function $$a$$ on the interval $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 126$$ . Its derivative is

section.heading: Applied Project The Calculus of Rainbows
section.paragraph: Rainbows are created when raindrops scatter sunlight. They have fascinated mankind since ancient times and have inspired attempts at scientific explanation since the time of Aristotle. In this project we use the ideas of Descartes and Newton to explain the shape, location, and colors of rainbows.

image.alt: Details An illustration shows a spherical raindrop and three points are marked on the circumference of the sphere: point A at the top left of the spherical drop; point B on the right side, and point C at the bottom. From the center of the spherical drop O, three dashed lines are drawn through the points A, B, and C. On the left side of the drop, the ray from the sun travels horizontally rightward and enters the spherical drop at the labeled point A. This ray makes an angle alpha with the extended line O A. It then travels down and to the right, and intersects the drop at point B, making an angle Beta with both the dashed lines O A and O B. From point B, the ray then travels down and to the left and intersects the drop at point C. This ray B C makes an angle Beta with both the dashed lines O B and O C. The ray then extends downward outside the spherical drop, but not as steep as ray B C, thus reflecting to an observer. This extended ray from point C makes an angle alpha with the extended dashed line O C. From point A, a dashed horizontal line extends rightward. From point C, a dashed line segment extends upward along with the extended downward slanting ray, goes up and to the right of ray B C, and meets the dashed horizontal line, making an obtuse angle D(alpha).

list.item: The figure shows a ray of sunlight entering a spherical raindrop at A. Some of the light is reflected, but the line AB shows the path of the part that enters the drop. Notice that the light is refracted toward the normal line AO and in fact Snell’s Law says that $$\sin\alpha = k\sin\beta$$ , where $$\alpha$$ is the angle of incidence, $$\beta$$ is the angle of refraction, and $$k \approx \frac{4}{3}$$ is the index of refraction for water. At B some of the light passes through the drop and is refracted into the air, but the line BC shows the part that is reflected. (The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.) When the ray reaches C, part of it is reflected, but for the time being we are more interested in the part that leaves the raindrop at C. (Notice that it is refracted away from the normal line.) The angle of deviation $$D(\alpha)$$ is the amount of clockwise rotation that the ray has undergone during this three-stage process. Thus $$D(\alpha) = \left( {\alpha - \beta} \right) + \left( {\pi - 2\beta} \right) + \left( {\alpha - \beta} \right) = \pi + 2\alpha - 4\beta$$ Show that the minimum value of the deviation is $$D(\alpha) \approx 138^{{^\circ}}$$ and occurs when $$\alpha \approx 59.4^{{^\circ}}$$ . The significance of the minimum deviation is that when $$\alpha \approx 59.4^{{^\circ}}$$ we have $$D^{\prime}(\alpha) \approx 0$$ , so $$\Delta D \slash \Delta\alpha \approx 0$$ . This means that many rays with $$\alpha \approx 59.4^{{^\circ}}$$ become deviated by approximately the same amount. It is the concentration of rays coming from near the direction of minimum deviation that creates the brightness of the primary rainbow. The figure below shows that the angle of elevation from the observer up to the highest point on the rainbow is $$180^{{^\circ}} - 138^{{^\circ}} = 42^{{^\circ}}$$ . (This angle is called the rainbow angle.) Details An illustration shows an observer on the ground on the left side and an arch-shaped rainbow on the right side with a few raindrops at its high point. A diagonal line connects the observer and the high point of the rainbow. A downward slanting ray, labeled rays from sun, passes through the observer from left to right, making an angle of 42 degrees with the diagonal line. Another downward slanting ray, labeled rays from sun, passes through the high point of the rainbow, parallel to the previous ray, making an angle of 138 degrees with the diagonal line, to the right of it. Two dashed lines from the observer connect the endpoints of the arch-shaped rainbow.

Problem 1 explains the location of the primary rainbow, but how do we explain the colors? Sunlight comprises a range of wavelengths, from the red range through orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. As Newton discovered in his prism experiments of 1666, the index of refraction is different for each color. (The effect is called dispersion.) For red light the refractive index is $$k \approx 1.3318$$ , whereas for violet light it is $$k \approx 1.3435$$ . By repeating the calculation of Problem 1 for these values of $$k$$ , show that the rainbow angle is about $$42.3^{{^\circ}}$$ for the red bow and $$40.6^{{^\circ}}$$ for the violet bow. So the rainbow really consists of seven individual bows corresponding to the seven colors. Details An illustration shows the spherical raindrop and four points are marked on the circumference of the sphere: point A at the bottom left; point B at the bottom right, a little above A; point C at the top right, and point D at the top left, a little below point C. A dashed line from point C extends downward to the left through point A. Another dashed line from point B extends upward to the left through point D. On the left side of the drop, a ray of light from the sun travels downward to the right and enters the circumference of the drop at point A, making an angle alpha with the extended line C A, outside the drop. From point A, the ray then travels upward to the right to point B, making an angle Beta with each of the extended lines C A and B D. From point B, the ray then travels upward to the left to point C, thus forming an angle Beta with each of the extended lines B D and C A. From point C, the ray then travels downward to the left to point D, making an angle Beta with each of the extended lines C A and B D. From point D, the ray then extends downward to the left to an observer, making an angle alpha with the extended line B D, outside the drop. Formation of the secondary rainbow

Perhaps you have seen a fainter secondary rainbow above the primary bow. That results from the part of a ray that enters a raindrop and is refracted at A, reflected twice (at B and C), and refracted as it leaves the drop at D (see the figure). This time the deviation angle $$D(\alpha)$$ is the total amount of counterclockwise rotation that the ray undergoes in this four-stage process. Show that $$D(\alpha) = 2\alpha - 6\beta + 2\pi$$ and $$D(\alpha)$$ has a minimum value when $$\cos\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{k^{2} - 1}{8}}$$ Taking $$k = \frac{4}{3}$$ , show that the minimum deviation is about $$129^{{^\circ}}$$ and so the rainbow angle for the secondary rainbow is about $$51^{{^\circ}}$$ , as shown in the figure below. Details An illustration shows an observer standing on the ground on the left side and observing two spherical raindrops that are vertically aligned on the right, in the air. The sun is located directly above the observer. Above the observer, a line segment extends downward to the right, passing through his head. Two rays from the sun pass through two spherical drops. One ray travels downward to the right to the bottom drop, reflects, and then travels down to the left to the observer, making an angle of 42 degrees with the line segment. Another ray travels downward to the right to the top drop, refracts, and then travels down to the left to the observer, making an angle of 51 degrees with the line segment.
Show that the colors in the secondary rainbow appear in the opposite order from those in the primary rainbow. Leonid Andronov / Shutterstock.com

note.title: Fermat
note.heading: Fermat
note.paragraph: Fermat’s Theorem is named after Pierre Fermat (1601–1665), a French lawyer who took up mathematics as a hobby. Despite his amateur status, Fermat was one of the two inventors of analytic geometry (Descartes was the other). His methods for finding tangents to curves and maximum and minimum values (before the invention of limits and derivatives) made him a forerunner of Newton in the creation of differential calculus.
